*Do-the-job track · Job C of 3.*

A daily return is ~unpredictable in its **mean** — but its **noise** is not.
Volatility *clusters*: turbulent days follow turbulent days.  So the move is to
**predict the noise** — forecast tomorrow's volatility from the past — and band
with it.  Deliverable: an interval that stays honest **in a crisis**, where a
single constant error bar fails.

---

## 1 · Forecast the Noise (Volatility)

The RiskMetrics EWMA forecast uses only the past, so it is a real one-step-ahead
prediction: $\sigma_t^2 = \lambda\,\sigma_{t-1}^2 + (1-\lambda)\,r_{t-1}^2$.

```{python}
R = datasets.load_returns()
r = R["JPM"].to_numpy(); dates = R.index

lam = 0.94
v = np.empty_like(r); v[0] = np.var(r[:20])
for t in range(1, len(r)):
    v[t] = lam * v[t - 1] + (1 - lam) * r[t - 1] ** 2   # causal: only the past
sigma_t = np.sqrt(v)

# Train the constant bar on the calm post-GFC, pre-COVID years; test on 2020+,
# so the COVID crisis is genuinely out of sample.
train = (dates >= "2012-01-01") & (dates < "2020-01-01")
te = np.where(dates >= "2020-01-01")[0]
const = r[train].std()                     # the one-number alternative
print(f"constant σ (calm 2012–19 train) : {const:.3f}")
print(f"forecast σ_t (2020+ test)       : {sigma_t[te].min():.3f} (calm) .. {sigma_t[te].max():.3f} (crisis)")
```

## 2 · Calibration — Where Each Band Holds

Returns are ~zero-mean, so the 95% interval is $\pm 1.96\,\sigma$.  Split the
out-of-sample days into calm and turbulent thirds and check coverage of each band.

```{python}
z = 1.96
st = sigma_t[te]
calm = te[st <= np.quantile(st, 1 / 3)]
turb = te[st >= np.quantile(st, 2 / 3)]

print(f"{'days':>16}  {'constant σ':>11}  {'forecast σ_t':>13}   (target 95%)")
for name, idx in [("all test", te), ("calm", calm), ("turbulent", turb)]:
    cov_c = np.mean(np.abs(r[idx]) <= z * const)
    cov_f = np.mean(np.abs(r[idx]) <= z * sigma_t[idx])
    print(f"{name:>16}  {cov_c:>11.0%}  {cov_f:>13.0%}")
```

The headline is the last row: on **turbulent days the constant band covers only
~79%** when it promises 95% — it gets pierced exactly in the crisis — while the
**forecast-σ band stays ~95%**.  Predicting the noise keeps the interval honest
when it matters most.

```{python}
#| label: fig-jobC-vol-band
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample JPM returns (2020 on). The forecast +/- 1.96 sigma_t band (blue) breathes with volatility and contains the crisis days; the constant +/- 1.96 sigma band (dashed), fixed on the calm 2012-19 years, is repeatedly pierced through the 2020 COVID stress."
te_dates = dates[te]
rt = r[te]; sg = sigma_t[te]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.8))
ax.fill_between(te_dates, -z * sg, z * sg, color=COOL, alpha=0.35,
                label="±1.96 σ̂$_t$  (forecast)")
ax.axhline(z * const, color=CRASH, lw=1.6, ls="--", label="±1.96 σ  (constant)")
ax.axhline(-z * const, color=CRASH, lw=1.6, ls="--")
ax.plot(te_dates, rt, c=INK, lw=0.5, alpha=0.8)
breach = np.abs(rt) > z * const
ax.scatter(te_dates[breach], rt[breach], s=14, c=CRASH, zorder=5,
           label="pierces constant band")
mark_event(ax, pd.Timestamp("2020-03-16"), "COVID")
ax.set_ylim(-0.18, 0.18); ax.set_ylabel("JPM daily return")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=9, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Deliverable
The calibration table is the report: a constant bar can look fine *on average* yet
fail in the tail, while a volatility forecast holds across regimes.  Even the
forecast band misses a touch more than nominal — fat tails; Gaussianize the
standardized residuals $r_t/\sigma_t$ (the Chapter-2 callback) to recover the last
points.
:::
